passage: Diary, Tuesday. Shalini. For weeks I'd been stuck on my thesis and kept saying to Kavitha, my mentor, "Could you give me a hand with something?" She'd say sure, and I'd freeze and say never mind. Today I wrote down exactly what I needed first. Then I said, "Ma'am, could you look at my second chapter's argument for twenty minutes on Thursday? I'm unsure whether the two examples support my claim." Kavitha smiled and wrote it in her calendar. I felt lighter, as if I'd been holding a heavy bag out at arm's length. On Thursday she pointed out the missing link in ten minutes. Being specific about what and when made it easy for her to help.

qa.q: What did Shalini ask Kavitha to look at?
qa.a: Shalini asked Kavitha to look at the second chapter's argument.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling before writing the request down?
qa.a: Shalini felt stuck and unsure, and froze whenever Kavitha said sure. The vague request left both of them unsure of the need.

qa.q: What did Shalini do that worked well?
qa.a: Shalini wrote down exactly what was needed and asked for a set time, which made it easy for Kavitha to say yes.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt about the earlier vague requests?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt unsure how to help, since Shalini kept saying 'never mind', and the specific request gave her something concrete to do.

grounding: A young adult requests help from a mentor by being specific about the need and time, whereas vague requests invite confusion.

passage:
Irfan: hey, could you give me a hand with something
Pooja: sure! what
Irfan: never mind, it's a lot
Pooja: ok?? now I'm curious. is it homework, a lift, something else?
Irfan: sorry that was vague. it's the maths assignment. can we do 30 mins on Saturday afternoon? I don't get question 4
Pooja: oh that I can do 🙂 3 pm at the library?
Irfan: yes! thank you. I'll bring what I tried
Pooja: perfect. when you just say "something" I don't know how to help
Irfan: fair. next time I'll say what and when
Pooja: 👍

qa.q: Which question did Irfan not understand?
qa.a: Irfan did not understand question 4.

qa.q: What did Pooja feel when Irfan said 'never mind, it's a lot'?
qa.a: Pooja felt curious and a little unsure how to help, since the request had no detail. Pooja then offered options to make it easier for Irfan to say what was needed.

qa.q: What did Irfan do that helped Pooja help?
qa.a: Irfan named the subject, asked for thirty minutes on Saturday afternoon and offered to bring the attempts so far.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when Pooja said vague requests were hard to answer?
qa.a: Irfan seems to have taken it well, perhaps a little sheepish about being vague, replying 'fair' and promising to say what and when next time.

grounding: A young adult requests help by naming the need and time, and vague requests invite confusion.

passage: The scholarship form was due at the block office in two days, and Ramesh was stuck on page three. He walked to the cyber café near the Kotputli bus stand, where Farhan, who helped half the village with forms, sat at his computer. "Farhan bhai, can you help me out?" Farhan, busy with three other customers, said, "Help with what? Come back in the evening." Ramesh went home, frustrated. That evening he tried again. This time he'd written it out. "Farhan bhai, I need help with section C of the state scholarship form, the income certificate upload. It's due Thursday. It'll take maybe fifteen minutes. Can you do it tonight or tomorrow morning?" Farhan looked at the paper, nodded and said, "Tomorrow, seven sharp, before the rush." At 7:15 the next morning the form was uploaded. Farhan grinned. "Why didn't you say that the first time?"

qa.q: Which section of the form was Ramesh stuck on?
qa.a: Section C, the income certificate upload.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when Farhan sent him away the first time?
qa.a: He felt frustrated, because his vague request didn't get him any help when he needed it.

qa.q: What made Ramesh's second request work?
qa.a: He named the exact section, the deadline, how long it would take, and offered two time options.

qa.q: How did Farhan see the two requests differently?
qa.a: The first was unclear while he was busy, so he put it off; the second was specific, so he could plan and say yes.

grounding: Shows a young adult getting help by making a specific request with the need and timeframe, after a vague request fails.

passage: Amara had three days until her dissertation chapter was due at the University of Leeds, and she was lost. She emailed her tutor, Dr Layla Hassan: "Hi, could you help me with my chapter? Thanks." The reply came the next morning: "Of course. What kind of help?" Amara stared at it. She didn't know herself. She spent an hour going through the chapter and found the real problem: her argument in section two didn't connect to her data. She wrote again: "Sorry, let me be clearer. I'm stuck on section two: my argument about housing policy doesn't link to the survey results. Could we meet for twenty minutes before Thursday? I can come Tuesday at 2 or Wednesday at 10." Dr Hassan replied within an hour: "Tuesday at 2. Bring the survey table." In the meeting, they fixed it in fifteen minutes. Amara walked out lighter.

qa.q: When did Dr Hassan agree to meet?
qa.a: Tuesday at 2.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling when she read "What kind of help?"?
qa.a: She felt stuck and a little embarrassed, because she didn't know herself what she needed.

qa.q: What made Amara's second email more useful?
qa.a: It named the exact problem, the section, a short meeting length, the deadline and two time options.

qa.q: How might Dr Hassan have felt reading the first, vague email?
qa.a: She was willing but unsure how to help, which is why she had to ask what kind of help Amara needed.

grounding: Shows a young adult turning a vague request for help into a specific one with need and timeframe, and getting help quickly.

passage: At the college counselling centre, Damini sat across from Nikita, the counsellor, and said, "I just... need help with stuff." Then silence. Nikita waited kindly. "Stuff can be a lot of things. Take your time." Damini twisted her dupatta. She had rehearsed nothing. "Exams, I guess. I'm not sleeping." "Tell me a bit more. What happens at night?" Damini found the words slowly. "I lie awake going over formulas. My first exam is in nine days. I want help to sleep better and to stop panicking in the exam hall." Nikita nodded and wrote it down. "That's very clear. Let's meet twice a week until your exams: Monday and Thursday at four. Today we'll start with one thing for sleep." Damini let out a breath. Walking out, she realised that saying exactly what she needed had made it feel smaller.

qa.q: When is Damini's first exam?
qa.a: In nine days.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling at the start of the session?
qa.a: She was anxious and unsure how to start, twisting her dupatta and saying only "stuff".

qa.q: How did Nikita help Damini make her request clearer?
qa.a: She waited kindly, asked open follow-ups about nights, and then set a clear plan with days and times.

qa.q: What would change if Damini had kept saying "stuff"?
qa.a: Nikita would have had to guess, and the session might have ended without a clear plan for sleep and exam panic.

grounding: Shows a young adult requesting help from a counsellor, moving from a vague request to a specific need and timeframe.

passage:
Subject: Specific help with my scholarship essay (before Friday)
Hi Shreya di,
Last week I messaged you "hey, could you help me out with a thing?" and then vanished, which wasn't fair. Sorry! Here's a proper ask.
I'm applying for the exchange programme scholarship, and the 500-word essay is due on Monday. I have a full draft. What I need is:
1. Twenty minutes of your time on a call, any evening before Friday.
2. Your honest view on paragraph two, where I explain why I switched from mechanical engineering to design. It sounds defensive to me and I can't see why.
I've attached the draft and highlighted that paragraph in yellow. If this week is too busy, just say so and I'll ask Professor Das instead. No hard feelings at all.
Thank you for being someone I can ask.
Manoj

qa.q: When is the essay due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel about last week's vague message?
qa.a: Manoj felt a little guilty and sheepish, since it asked for help without saying what, and then vanished.

qa.q: What makes this new request easy to say yes to?
qa.a: It names the exact help, the time needed and the deadline, attaches the draft with the paragraph highlighted, and gives an easy way to say no 🙂

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt receiving last week's "hey, could you help me out with a thing?"
qa.a: Probably puzzled, unsure what was needed or how much time it would take.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult replacing a vague request for help with a specific ask that states the need, the time and the deadline.
